subject: English 1st Paper
topic: Lesson-01: Going to a new school

source.edition: Revised for the year 2026; revised edition October 2025

passagePolicy: Use the textbook Section A form (printed 1), Section B narrative (printed 2) and Section C poem (printed 3). They are distinct source units, not one invented combined passage. Questions require the cited book pages; the complete textbook texts are not reproduced here.

activities.instruction: Read the source unit cited for each question and select the best answer.

items.question: Why did the teacher give Tarun a form?

options.B: To choose a train for him
options.C: To give him a football prize

items.explanation: The introduction states the teacher wanted to know more about him.

items.question: Which pair contains Tarun's hobbies?
items.explanation: His form distinguishes hobbies from the activities he is good at.

items.question: What does Tarun say he dislikes?
items.explanation: The last statement in his form identifies soft drinks.

items.question: How did Tarun travel to school on his first day?
items.explanation: The narrative names both the vehicle and his companion.

items.question: How long did the journey to school take?
items.explanation: The passage states that they reached school after fifteen minutes.

items.question: What did Tarun do after entering the classroom?

options.A: He went back to the gate

items.explanation: Finding a seat follows entering the classroom in the narrative.

items.question: Which detail supports the idea that Tarun met a welcoming class?

options.C: The pupils were friendly and the teacher greeted the class warmly
options.D: He had moved to a city

items.explanation: The welcome is supported by classroom behaviour, not travel details.

activities.instruction: Answer using the cited part of Lesson 1. Equivalent accurate wording is acceptable.

items.question: Why was Tarun going to a new school?
items.modelAnswer: He had moved to a new city with his parents.

items.question: Name two activities Tarun says he is good at.
items.modelAnswer: He is good at playing football and drawing.

items.question: Where did Tarun's father leave him?
items.modelAnswer: His father said goodbye and left him at the school gate.

items.question: What had the other pupils done before Tarun entered?
items.modelAnswer: They had already gone to class.

items.question: How did the teacher and pupils help make his first day pleasant?
items.modelAnswer: The teacher greeted the class warmly, and Tarun found the pupils very friendly. These actions gave him a welcoming experience.

activities.instruction: Complete these notes about Tarun using the word box. Use each word once.
activities.text: Tarun is (a) ____ years old. His eyes are (b) ____. He is good at football and (c) ____. One of his hobbies is (d) ____. On his first school day, his father left him at the school (e) ____.
activities.note: Cross-section lesson practice, not Q3 from one continuous model-test passage.

activities.instruction: Give the requested meaning in the cited context. Accept suitable alternatives.
Read “Let's Play” in Lesson 1 Section C and answer the eight practice questions. Do not treat all eight as compulsory in a model test.

items.question: Who wrote the poem presented as “Let's Play” in this lesson?
items.assessmentGuide: Names the credited poet, without attributing authorship to the textbook editors.

items.question: When does the play in the poem begin?
items.modelAnswer: It begins after school is over and lessons have finished.
items.assessmentGuide: Connects play with the end of lessons.

items.question: What two playful challenges appear in the poem?
items.modelAnswer: The children wonder who will run fastest and who will laugh loudest.

items.question: What mood does the poem create? Give a supporting detail.
items.modelAnswer: It creates a joyful, playful mood. The children welcome the end of school and invite one another to run and laugh.
items.assessmentGuide: Names a plausible mood and supports it from the text.

items.question: Who are included in the words “you or I”?
items.modelAnswer: The speaker and the person being addressed are included. The poem does not identify their individual names.

items.question: How does the ending encourage participation?
items.modelAnswer: The invitation to try suggests that both children can join the activity rather than only watch it.
items.assessmentGuide: Explains the inclusive invitation; does not claim a winner is named.

items.question: What is the effect of the question marks in the poem?
items.modelAnswer: They mark the questions about who will run fastest and laugh loudest, making the challenges sound lively.
items.assessmentGuide: Connects punctuation with the two questions.

items.question: Does the poem tell us who wins the running challenge? Explain.
items.modelAnswer: No. It raises the challenge and invites the children to try, but does not report a result.
items.assessmentGuide: Distinguishes an invitation from a reported outcome.

activities.note: The book sample offers eight poem questions, with any five answered. These are a lesson practice pool, not a claim that this poem must be selected nationally.

activities.instruction: Write a paragraph of 120 words about your first day at school. Describe your feelings and explain them.
activities.modelAnswer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.
activities.lengthBasis: 120 words follows the textbook sample Q12 (printed 105 / PDF 110), not a separately verified current national circular.
assessment: Relevant first-person account with reasons for feelings
Appropriate punctuation and the requested length
activities.note: Original personal-writing example, not facts about Tarun. Students may use different experiences; do not require verbatim memorisation.
